claim: Israel is trying to wipe out the Palestinians of Gaza.

answer: Gaza had about 2.2 million people before the war. Its health ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, counts over 72,000 dead, about 3 per cent, without separating civilians from fighters. Israel warned civilians to leave areas, agreed to pauses for a 2024 polio campaign, and says it let in large amounts of aid. Against that: a full aid ban from 2 March to 19 May 2025, a famine finding in August 2025, 81 per cent of structures damaged, most people displaced, and officials' statements the ICJ quoted. Amnesty, a UN commission, B'Tselem, PHRI and genocide scholars concluded Israel committed genocide; Israel, the US government and some legal scholars reject that. Our reading: the record is mixed, so we do not say the intent test is met. The ICJ has not ruled, and the bodies named above concluded otherwise.

facts.text: Israel's military issued evacuation warnings before operations in Gaza; a BBC analysis of 26 warnings found they contained specific information people could use to escape, but that 17 also contained errors and inconsistencies. The court used them to find the Palestinians' right to protection plausible and did not rule on intent.

contested: The bodies that concluded Israel is committing or has committed genocide, in full: Amnesty International (December 2024), the UN Commission of Inquiry (16 September 2025, which says it does not speak for the UN as a whole), B'Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights Israel (28 July 2025), and the International Association of Genocide Scholars (resolution of 31 August 2025, 86 per cent of the 28 per cent of its roughly 500 members who voted). Individual legal scholars, quoted by LTO (August 2025), go further: Itamar Mann (Haifa) concludes the only reasonable inference is genocidal intent, dating it to February 2025; another scholar there says that as of August 2025 there is a strong case that it is the only reasonable inference even if it was not at earlier points. A. Dirk Moses and Fyfe (NPR, September 2025) argue the pattern of destruction cannot be explained as collateral damage and that the siege has no clear military purpose.

Those who dispute it: Israel's government (it told the ICJ the specific intent has not been shown, called the Commission's report 'distorted and false', called B'Tselem's report politically motivated and the IAGS resolution 'an embarrassment to the legal profession'); the US State Department called Amnesty's allegation 'unfounded' (December 2024); in a declaration of intervention at the ICJ dated 12 March 2026 the United States, as summarised by Opinio Juris, relied on Israel's efforts to comply with the laws of armed conflict and to mitigate civilian harm as evidence that genocide is not a reasonable inference. We did not read the declaration itself. Stefan Talmon says war crimes are likely but genocidal intent is not proved.

Timing. The scholars above do not agree on when, or whether, intent could be inferred; the pattern changes over the period (heavy fighting, the January to March 2025 ceasefire, the March to May 2025 blockade, the August 2025 famine finding, the October 2025 ceasefire and after). A reader should not read the card as describing one uniform period. After the ceasefire of October 2025 the IPC found no famine (December 2025), but Gaza's health ministry still reports hundreds killed since, and Israel's military still holds over half the territory (UN OCHA, 15 October 2026 and 2025 reports).

The counts. The death toll comes from the Gaza Health Ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, which does not say how many were fighters; Israel has dismissed the ministry's figures as Hamas propaganda, while the UN and the Associated Press have treated the overall total as generally reliable. The IPC famine finding is disputed by Israel's COGAT, which cites its own aid figures and says the IPC relies on gaps in data; the UN counts and COGAT counts of aid trucks differ and have not been reconciled.

The ICJ's January 2024 order found the Palestinians' right to protection from genocide plausible, which is a low provisional threshold; it did not find that genocide was committed or that Israel's intent was genocidal, and its then-president said it did not decide that the genocide claim itself was plausible. The first measure was passed by fifteen votes to two; judge Sebutinde and judge ad hoc Barak voted against. The statements by Israeli officials the court quoted were made in October 2023; the court did not say they showed intent.

What warnings and pauses show is itself disputed: Israel and some legal commentators treat evacuation warnings and humanitarian pauses as evidence of efforts to protect civilians; Amnesty and others say that ordering people to move to places that were then attacked, or with nowhere safe to go, cannot be an effective warning and may amount to forced displacement. Evidence of such efforts can count against genocidal intent, but does not make an attack lawful.
could_not_verify: A third independent source for Gaza's pre-war population: the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics release is a PDF the checker cannot read, and the US government page that quotes it counts as a government source. UN OCHA and the BBC are the reliable sources.

The latest death toll. Reports in September to November 2026 give about 74,000 to 74,700, but the Associated Press pages refused the checker and the other pages I found were not reliable enough to cite; the card uses the OCHA figure of 11 February 2026 and the Independent's mid-June 2026 report.
The share of the dead who were fighters. I found no independent count; Israel's own claims about militants killed were not read, and the UN and the ministry give no split.
The outcome of the 2024 polio campaign (the coverage reached) was not checked; the card states only the agreement for pauses. The Reuters report of the agreement refused the checker.

Israel's own totals for aid (COGAT dashboard, Israeli foreign ministry) are PDFs the checker cannot read; they are cited only through Ynetnews and the BBC. Israel's stated reason for the March to May 2025 blockade (the prime minister's office said aid would not enter until Hamas released the hostages, per a Reuters report that refused the checker) is therefore not on the card.
The IPC's 2023 and 2024 findings (risk of famine, the Famine Review Committee's reviews of 2024) were not read; the card covers only the August and December 2025 findings.
The full B'Tselem and PHRI reports, the Commission of Inquiry report and the IAGS resolution were not read; the card relies on press releases, summaries and news coverage.

Statements by Israeli officials after January 2024 (including proposals about the departure of Gaza's residents, cited by IAGS and by scholars) are not on the card; nor did I find whether Israel investigated or disowned the October 2023 statements the ICJ quoted.

Evacuation-warning figures given by the Israeli military (leaflets, text messages, calls) came only from a think-tank page that I did not treat as reliable; the Washington Post report refused the checker.

Facts with only two reliable sources (the rest have three): the pre-war population (OCHA and the BBC, plus a US government page); Israel's account to the ICJ (the ICJ and the Indian Express); the B'Tselem and PHRI finding (NPR and ABC, plus B'Tselem itself as an advocacy source); the Talmon fact (Euronews and LTO); and the ICJ-has-not-ruled fact (BBC and The Citizen, plus the South African government).
not_claimed: This card does not say the conduct was lawful. Famine, blocked aid and the destruction of housing are not defended here, and nothing on the card says they were justified.

It does not say civilians were not killed in very large numbers. About 3 per cent of Gaza's pre-war population is reported dead by the ministry that counts them, and the UN treats the total as broadly reliable.
It does not say that war crimes did not occur. Even a scholar who rejects the genocide finding (Talmon) says the starvation of civilians as a method of war is a war crime.
It does not say the ICJ has found genocide or has rejected the claim; it has not ruled.
It does not say that Amnesty, the UN Commission, B'Tselem, PHRI or the genocide scholars are wrong, or that Israel's rejection is right.
